v1.0.0 (2026-10-16) first version, from latent-season10-bible-v1.0.1.md row a10e04, writer brief a10e04-v1.0.0.md, LATENT catalog v1.0.77 and latent-syllabus-v1.0.3.md. a10e03's next field was honoured: a tannery working through the night, how several answers share each step on the card, why a batch that starts and ends together keeps short answers waiting for the longest, and letting answers join and leave after every step. Keeps apart from Dead Letter s9e16 (one pass per photo with a fill wait; here generation, answers of different lengths, no wait to fill a batch, no robots), from a6e04 (a provider's cheaper overnight queue), from a8e02 (hides and drums, no sewing or clothes), from the retired ferry setting and from a10e01's furnace. Shared given data: Llama 3.1 8B, 16.06 billion bytes in 16 bits, about 15 GB on the card's meter; A100 80GB 2,039 GB/s, H100 3.35 TB/s; sizes in the meter's units, speeds in the maker's. The tannery's own measurements, never a source's: the writing curve, 10 ms a step plus 0.25 ms per answer in it (1: 10.25 ms; 4: 11; 8: 12; 16: 14), and the log times. Story arithmetic (all in sims/a10e04-v1.0.0.js): the old program runs 8 places, filled or not, so every step is 12 ms; a 40-token answer 40 x 12 ms = 0.48 s in a batch (0.41 s alone at 10.25 ms); 02:00:00.0 the report (2,000 tokens) and 7 drum screens (40 tokens each) start batch 1, 2,000 x 12 ms = 24.0 s; drum 6 typed at 02:00:00.6 and drum 11 at 02:00:05.0 (4 tokens) run in batch 2 from 24.0 s to 24.48 s: 23.88, 23.9 s, and 19.48, 19.5 s (the brief's 24 - 5 + 0.48); places doing work (7 x 40 + 2,000) / (8 x 2,000) = 14%; after every step: screens 0.48 s, drum 6 0.42 s, drum 11 0.04 s, the report 20.6 s (no longer 24 s, because steps with fewer answers are quicker), 100%; batches of 4 (11 ms): drum 6 22.3 s, drum 11 17.9 s, the report's batch 22.0 s; H100 (7.3 ms): 14.6 s, drum 6 14.3 s, drum 11 9.9 s; report capped at 500 tokens: 6.0 s, drum 6 5.9 s; A10 $1.29 x 730 = $942 a month; A100 $2.79 x 730 = $2,037; H100 $3.99 to $4.29, $2,913 to $3,132. One deliberate change from the brief: the brief's record put drum 6 at 23.9 s inside the report's batch, which cannot be (every member of a 24.0 s batch waits at least 24.0 s), so drum 6 is typed at 02:00:00.6 and runs in the next batch; the 7 short answers in the report's batch wait 24.0 s. Timeline: the program written in 2025; the report on its own A10 until Monday 5 October 2026, moved that day; first run on the shared server 02:00 on Tuesday 6 October; at midnight drum 6's same question took 0.48 s; Thorvaldur called the storyteller over at about 02:00:20; the post at about 06:00 on Tuesday 6 October; the next report run 02:00 on Wednesday 7 October. Cold case: 2 months later, 6 October to Sunday 6 December 2026 (the fix live from Wednesday 7 October; eight reports from Monday 2 November; the night of Tuesday 1 December): 8 reports fill all 8 places, drum 6 23.9 s and drum 11 19.5 s again; with 16 places drum 6 0.50 s, screens 0.55 s, reports 24.1 s. Standards note conditional, not legal advice. Sources read 16 October 2026.
title: Many at Once
setting: a tannery working through the night

post.author: u/drum_room_bogumila
post.title: I run the night drums at a tannery. At 02:00 our assistant wrote seven answers in half a second, then held them back for 23.5 seconds more.

blocks.text: I'm Bogumila, night drum operator at Wrangthorpe Tannery. All night, hides turn in twelve drums, rotating wooden barrels, through timed chemical steps; the chrome step turns hide into leather. Eight of us run them.

Each drum has a screen. When the night plan moves a drum to its next step, its screen asks our assistant how long that step runs. We type our own questions too: "drum 6: how long after the chrome step?" Most answers run 30 to 60 tokens, the small pieces of text a language model writes.
Ours is Llama 3.1 8B. It runs on one rented graphics card, a card for short: an NVIDIA A100 80GB, $2.79 an hour.
Its weights, its learned numbers, take 16.06 billion bytes, about 15 GB, billions of bytes, on the card's meter. The card and the program that feeds it make up our server.

The model writes in steps. In each step the card reads all 16.06 billion bytes along its memory road, 2,039 GB a second: at least 7.9 ms, thousandths of a second. Every answer in the step gets one more token from that one read.
Answers share steps cheaply. Our own timing: a step takes 10 ms plus 0.25 ms per answer in it. Alone, 10.25 ms; eight together, 12 ms.

Rasmussen in IT wrote our program last year. First it collects up to 8 waiting questions. Then it runs them together, step by step, always in 8 places, filled or not. It returns every answer when the longest ends. Anything asked meanwhile waits for the next round.

Like a group at a ticket counter that can't leave until its slowest member is served. Engineers call such a group a batch, and this way static batching. A 40-token answer in a batch: 40 steps of 12 ms, 0.48 s. Alone it could take 0.41 s.

Every night at 02:00 the assistant also writes the drum-log report for Hippolyta, our chemist: 2,000 tokens. It ran on its own small card, an A10, at $1.29 an hour, $942 a month. On Monday 5 October Rasmussen moved it onto our server to save that. Tonight, Tuesday 6 October, was its first run.
Each line: time, event, each answer's first words and wait.

02:00:00.0  report + 7 drum screens ask; batch 1 starts, 8 of 8
02:00:00.6  drum 6 asks; waits
02:00:05.0  drum 11 asks; waits
02:00:24.0  batch 1 ends: report and 7 screens  after 24.0 s
02:00:24.5  drum 6   "Drum 6: 40 minutes. Then..."  after 23.9 s
02:00:24.5  drum 11  "Not yet."  after 19.5 s
Thorvaldur, waiting on drum 6's timing, called me over to a screen that had spun for twenty seconds. At midnight the same question took 0.48 s.

blocks.label: two_am_batches.png

diagram.aria: Bogumila's drawing of 02:00:00 to 02:00:26 on the shared server. Row one, the drum-log report: writing from 0 to 24 seconds. Row two, the 7 drum screens: written by 0.48 seconds, then held, finished, until 24 seconds. Row three, drum 6: asked at 0.6 seconds, waiting until 24 seconds, then written by 24.48 seconds. Row four, drum 11: asked at 5 seconds, waiting until 24 seconds, then answered at 24.48 seconds. Markers at 0.48 seconds, screens written, and 24 seconds, batch 1 ends.

blocks.caption: Drawn at 05:30 from the server's log. Batch 1 held the report and the 7 drum screens. The screens' answers were written by 0.48 s and held, finished, until the report's 2,000th step at 24.0 s. Drum 6 and drum 11 asked after batch 1 began, so they waited for it to end, then ran 40 steps of 12 ms in batch 2.

blocks.text: By hand: the report needs 2,000 steps × 12 ms = 24 s. Its 7 screen answers were done at 0.48 s and waited out the rest. Drum 6: 24.0 - 0.6 + 0.48 = 23.9 s. Drum 11: 24.0 - 5 + 0.48 = 19.5 s.
Places doing work in batch 1: (7 × 40 + 2,000) ÷ (8 × 2,000) = 14%. Of 24 paid seconds, 23.5 went on writing one answer in eight places.
Rasmussen says batching is batching; the report needs a smaller batch. It runs again at 02:00 tomorrow. What should we change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in your drum room is haunted, though a screen that spins in the dark is grim. Engineers call each of your program's 8 places a slot. Your 12 ms step is also the gap between one token and the next for every answer in it, the inter-token latency, ITL for short (a10e02). Two questions. At step 41 of batch 1, how many of the 8 slots were still writing? And when did drum 11's wait begin and end, and what was it waiting for?

replies.author: u/drum_room_bogumila
replies.text: One. The report. The other 7 slots held finished answers. Drum 11 asked at 02:00:05 and waited until batch 1 ended at 02:00:24.0, for the report's last token, then 0.48 s in batch 2.

comments.author: u/batching_is_batching_rasmussen
comments.text: I wrote the program. Batching is batching: one read of the weights for 8 answers is the only reason one card copes with all of us. Keeping a batch together is simple, and it has never lost an answer. Newer serving programs re-pack the batch after every step: finished answers leave, waiting ones take their slots, then the next step runs. That's a lot of moving parts on a night shift. The report is just big. Give it a smaller batch: cap batches at 4, so fewer answers ever sit behind it, and stop fiddling with the server.

replies.author: u/drum_room_bogumila
replies.text: With 4, how many steps does the report's batch still run?

replies.author: u/batching_is_batching_rasmussen
replies.text: The same 2,000. But three answers stuck with it, not seven.

comments.author: u/night_chemist_hippolyta
comments.text: I read the drum log at 06:00 and set the day's chrome from it. Before Monday it ran on its own A10 and nobody's screen waited for it. $942 a month is cheap next to a drum drained too early. Give it its card back. And don't trim my report to 500 tokens to make it fit; I need every drum's log.

replies.author: u/drum_room_bogumila
replies.text: The A10 did one job a night, the 2,000-token report, and sat idle the rest of the day.

comments.author: u/works_manager_wilbrord
comments.text: Simplest fix: a faster card. An H100 moves 3.35 TB a second, terabytes, thousands of GB, against the A100's 2,039 GB. Same program, same batches, every step shorter. I'd rather buy speed than buy complexity.

reply.prompt: It's 06:00 on Tuesday 6 October, and the report runs again at 02:00 tomorrow. What should the tannery change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Cut each batch to 4 questions so fewer answers wait behind the report.
options.part2: On Tuesday Rasmussen set the program to 4 places, and Wednesday's 02:00 came in just as Tuesday's had. Steps took 11 ms now, and the report's batch, with drums 1 to 3, still ran 2,000 of them: 22.0 s. Drums 4, 5, 7 and 8 waited for the second batch and answered after 22.4 s. Thorvaldur's drum 6 question came back after 22.3 s, drum 11's after 17.9 s. Three answers sat behind the report instead of seven, and everyone else queued behind those.
options.senior: A smaller batch changes how many answers share the long one's fate, not the fate. A batch that starts and ends together still runs as many steps as its longest answer, 2,000 here, and everything that arrives meanwhile waits for it to end. Fewer places also means fewer answers per read of the weights, so the card does less work per step. The fault is when answers may leave and join, not how many there are.

options.text: Let finished answers leave after every step and waiting ones join.
options.part2: On Tuesday Rasmussen swapped the program for vLLM, a free serving engine that re-packs its batch after every step, on the same card, still 8 slots. By 18:00 they had replayed Tuesday's 02:00 in the sim. At 02:00 on Wednesday the report and the 7 screens started together. The screens' answers left after step 40, 0.48 s. Thorvaldur's drum 6 question took a free slot at the next step and came back after 0.42 s; drum 11's after 0.04 s. The report reached Hippolyta after 20.6 s, sooner than before, because steps with fewer answers are quicker. No screen spun, and every slot in every step was writing.
options.senior: Schedule by the step, not by the batch. After every step, return the answers that are finished, fill their slots from the queue, then run the next step: iteration-level scheduling, which Orca introduced and vLLM does by default as continuous batching. Short answers no longer wait for long ones, and no slot spends steps holding a finished answer: 14% of slots doing work becomes 100%. It costs a smarter program, and when every slot is full, newcomers still queue for the first free one.

options.text: Give the drum-log report its own small card back, as before Monday.
options.part2: On Tuesday the report went back to its own A10. At 02:00 on Wednesday the screens answered after 0.48 s, Thorvaldur's drum 6 after 0.48 s and drum 11 after 0.05 s, as at midnight. Hippolyta had the report at 06:00. The A10 is back on the bill, $942 a month, for one job a night; it sits idle more than 23 hours a day. And the shared server still holds every answer until its batch's longest ends, so the next long job anyone adds will bring the wait back.
options.senior: An honest trade. Keeping the long job off the shared server removes the wait tonight and costs $942 a month for a card that is idle nearly all day. It hides the scheduling fault rather than fixing it: the old program still holds short answers for the longest in their batch, and any longer answer, a long question from an operator or a second report, brings the wait back.

options.text: Move the shared server to a faster card so the long report ends sooner.
options.part2: IT rented an H100 at $3.99 to $4.29 a card hour on the same price list: $2,913 to $3,132 a month instead of $2,037. Each step took 7.3 ms. At 02:00 on Wednesday the report's batch ran 14.6 s. The screens' answers were written in 0.29 s and held for the rest; Thorvaldur's drum 6 came back after 14.3 s, drum 11 after 9.9 s. Every number shrank by the ratio of the two memory roads, and every short answer still waited for the longest.
options.senior: A faster memory road shortens every step by the same ratio, 2,039 ÷ 3,350 here, so a 24 s wait becomes about 15. The shape stays: short answers held for the longest in their batch, newcomers waiting for the batch to end, 14% of slots doing work. You pay more an hour for the same waste, done faster. Fix how the batch is scheduled before buying speed.

sim.title: Replay 02:00 on the tannery's shared server
sim.lede: You're Bogumila at 01:59:50 on Tuesday 6 October, ten seconds before the drum-log report's first run on the shared server. No real model runs here: every figure is worked out from given numbers. Given: Llama 3.1 8B, 16.06 billion bytes of weights, read once a step; the A100 80GB's memory road moves 2,039 GB a second, an H100's 3.35 TB. The tannery's own timing on its A100: a step takes 10 ms plus 0.25 ms per answer in it (on an H100 the sim shortens every step by 2,039 ÷ 3,350). The old program runs up to 8 answers in 8 places, filled or not, and returns them all when the longest ends; the new way lets finished answers leave and waiting ones join after every step. At 02:00:00.0 the report (2,000 tokens) and 7 drum screens (40 tokens each) ask together, the report first; Thorvaldur types drum 6's question (40 tokens) at 02:00:00.6, and drum 11's two-word answer (4 tokens) is asked at 02:00:05. The story's log shows only each answer's first words. Prices per card hour, from one provider's list: A100 $2.79, A10 $1.29, H100 $3.99 to $4.29; a month is 730 hours.
sim.tryThis: Try this: the opening view is 02:00 as it will run: 12 ms steps, the screens written at 0.48 s and returned at 24.0 s, drum 6 after 23.9 s, drum 11 after 19.5 s, 14% of places doing work. Play 02:00. Switch to 4 places, then to an H100, then trim the report to 500 tokens: every wait shrinks, none goes. Move the report to its own A10 and watch the bill. Then schedule after every step. Last, set 8 reports at 02:00 with the new scheduling and see what fills the slots, then try 16 places. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the drum room was haunted. The old program returns a batch's answers together when its longest ends, so the 2,000-token report held its batch for 2,000 steps of 12 ms, 24.0 s. The 7 screens' answers, done at 0.48 s, sat in their slots for the rest, and drum 6 and drum 11, asked after it began, waited for it to end: 23.9 s and 19.5 s.

steps.title: A step: one read of the weights, one token for every answer in it.
steps.text: First, the card reads all 16.06 billion bytes of weights along its memory road, at 2,039 GB a second: at least 7.9 ms. Second, it works out the next token for every answer in the step. Third, each answer gets that token, and the step is done. Because the read is shared, more answers cost little: on the tannery's own timing a step takes 10 ms plus 0.25 ms per answer, 10.25 ms alone, 12 ms for eight. A 40-token answer takes 40 steps: 0.48 s among eight, 0.41 s alone. What can go wrong: thinking each answer pays for its own read, and so running answers one at a time.

steps.title: Static batching: start together, end together.
steps.text: First, the old program collects up to 8 waiting questions. Second, it runs them together in 8 slots, filled or not, step after step. Third, it returns every answer when the longest has its last token. Fourth, anything asked meanwhile waits for the next batch. So a batch moves at the pace of its longest answer. At 02:00 the report needed 2,000 steps × 12 ms = 24.0 s; the 7 screens were written by 0.48 s and held to 24.0 s; drum 6 waited 24.0 - 0.6 + 0.48 = 23.9 s and drum 11 24.0 - 5 + 0.48 = 19.5 s. Slots doing work: (7 × 40 + 2,000) ÷ (8 × 2,000) = 14%. What can go wrong: one long answer holds seven short ones and everyone behind them.

steps.title: Why it never showed before.
steps.text: Until Monday every answer on the shared server ran 30 to 60 tokens, so the answers in a batch ended within a few steps of each other, and the longest held the rest for a fraction of a second. The 2,000-token report ran on its own A10, where nobody waited behind it. Moving it saved $1.29 × 730 = $942 a month and put the first long answer into batches built for short ones. Dead Letter's s9e16 batched photos that each needed one pass and waited to fill a batch; here every answer needs as many steps as it has tokens, and their lengths differ. What can go wrong: a change that looks like saving a card is really a change in who waits for whom.

steps.title: Leaving and joining after every step.
steps.text: First, run one step for every answer in a slot. Second, return any answer that has its last token. Third, fill the free slots from the waiting questions, oldest first. Fourth, run the next step. Yu and colleagues' Orca paper calls this iteration-level scheduling; it also batches only the parts of each step that can be shared (selective batching), since answers of different lengths can't be stacked for every part. vLLM does it by default and calls it continuous batching. Replayed: the screens leave at 0.48 s, drum 6 joins at the next step and leaves after 0.42 s, drum 11 after 0.04 s, and the report takes 20.6 s, because steps with fewer answers are quicker. What can go wrong: when every slot holds a long answer, a newcomer still waits for the first free slot.

steps.title: Why the other fixes fall short.
steps.text: Batches of 4 make each step 11 ms but the report's batch still runs 2,000 steps, 22.0 s; drum 6 waits 22.3 s and drum 11 17.9 s. An H100's road, 3,350 GB a second, shortens every step to 7.3 ms: the report's batch 14.6 s, drum 6 14.3 s, for $2,913 to $3,132 a month instead of $2,037. A 500-token report makes it 6.0 s, drum 6 5.9 s, and the chemist loses three-quarters of the drum log. The A10 back removes the wait for $942 a month and leaves the fault in place. What can go wrong: shrinking the wait and calling it gone.

diagram.aria: Two ways to run 02:00 on one card. Top row, static batching: at 02:00 the report and 7 screens start in 8 slots; steps 1 to 40, 8 answers write, 12 ms a step; steps 41 to 2,000, 1 writes and 7 hold finished answers, 14% of slots at work; all returned at 24.0 s, drum 6 after 23.9 s. Bottom row, after every step: the same start; after step 40 the 7 screens leave at 0.48 s; drum 6 joins a free slot and is answered after 0.42 s; the report is returned at 20.6 s with every slot writing.

notes.text: Static: the batch ends with its longest answer, 2,000 x 12 ms
After every step: finished answers leave, waiting ones join
One read of the weights per step serves every slot

explain.caption: Read each row left to right. Static batching starts the report and the 7 screens together and returns them together, so the screens' answers, done at 0.48 s, wait in their slots until the report's 2,000th step at 24.0 s. Scheduling after every step lets the screens leave at 0.48 s and gives drum 6 a free slot at once.

fix.title: The fix: let finished answers leave and waiting ones join after every step
fix.text: Serve the model with an engine that schedules by the step, such as vLLM, which does continuous batching by default, on the same A100. After every step it returns finished answers and fills their slots from the queue, so the screens' answers come back in about half a second while the report writes on beside them. Replay the 02:00 traffic in the sim before the switch. Then watch two numbers each night: how long the longest short answer waited, and how many questions waited for a free slot, and tell the night operators when either rises. Before adding any long job to the shared server, check whether it can fill every slot at once.

limits: Leaving and joining after every step needs a free slot. When long answers fill every slot, as eight reports at once would, a short question waits for the first to finish; more slots, or slots kept for short answers, are the cure.

Each extra answer in a step adds 0.25 ms on the tannery's curve and keeps its own working memory on the card (a10e03), so slots are not free. The curve and the log times are the tannery's own measurements; another card or model needs its own.
A real engine also reads each new question before writing (a10e02), and long questions read in the middle of others' writing can slow their steps. The sim counts every step at the curve's cost.
explain.seniorTake: A generating model writes one token per step for every answer in the step, and one read of the weights serves them all, which is why serving many at once is cheap. How you schedule that sharing decides who waits. Static batching starts a batch together and returns it together, so it moves at the pace of its longest answer: fine while answers are short and alike, ruinous the night one long answer joins. One long answer held seven short ones and everyone behind them, and 86% of the card's slots spent 23.5 seconds doing nothing useful. Scheduling after every step, iteration-level scheduling or continuous batching, returns each answer the moment it is done and fills its slot from the queue, so short answers stop waiting for long ones and the card's steps carry only real work. Smaller batches and faster cards shrink the wait without removing it; a separate card removes it at a monthly price. Then size the slots for the busiest moment, because a full set of long answers still makes newcomers queue.

realWorld.title: Orca: why batches that end together hurt
realWorld.text: Yu and colleagues' Orca paper (OSDI '22) says existing serving systems use an inflexible scheduling mechanism that cannot change the current batch of requests being processed, so requests that have finished earlier than other requests in a batch cannot return to the client, while newly arrived requests have to wait until the current batch completely finishes. That is the tannery's 02:00.

realWorld.title: Orca: iteration-level scheduling and selective batching
realWorld.text: The same paper proposes iteration-level scheduling, which schedules execution at the granularity of iteration (instead of request), to run only a single iteration of the model on the batch, and selective batching, which applies batching only to a selected set of operations, so answers of different lengths can still share a step.

realWorld.title: Orca: 36.9 times the throughput
realWorld.text: On a GPT-3 175B model the paper reports Orca against NVIDIA's FasterTransformer at a 36.9× throughput improvement at the same level of latency. The USENIX page prints it as 36:9×, a typesetting slip; the figure is 36.9. It was measured on their model and cards, not the tannery's.

realWorld.title: vLLM: continuous batching by default
realWorld.text: vLLM's documentation home lists, among what it is fast with, Continuous batching of incoming requests, chunked prefill, prefix caching. The tannery's fix uses the first of those; a10e03's pages are the PagedAttention line above it.

realWorld.title: What the cards cost
realWorld.text: Lambda's pricing page, read on 16 October 2026, lists the NVIDIA A10 with 24 GB at $1.29 per GPU per hour, the A100 SXM with 80 GB (SXM is the board form the card is built in) at $2.79 and the H100 SXM at $3.99 to $4.29 depending on the machine size. At 730 hours a month the A10 is $942 and the A100 $2,037. Prices change; the arithmetic is the lesson.

realWorld.title: A100: the memory road the steps wait on
realWorld.text: NVIDIA's A100 page gives the A100 80GB SXM a GPU memory bandwidth of 2,039 GB/s. Reading 16.06 billion bytes at that speed takes at least 7.9 ms, which is why the tannery's steps start at 10 ms and a batch's cost is mostly that one read.

realWorld.title: H100: a wider road, the same wait
realWorld.text: NVIDIA's H100 page gives the H100 SXM a GPU memory bandwidth of 3.35TB/s. Every step shrinks by 2,039 ÷ 3,350, so the report's batch drops from 24.0 s to 14.6 s; static batching still holds every short answer for it.

asked: What is continuous batching and why does it beat static batching for LLMs?
How would you serve short chats and long reports on one GPU?
interview.answer: A model writes one token per step for every answer in the step, and the step's cost is mostly one read of the weights, so batching many answers is nearly free per answer: on one A100 I've seen 10.25 ms for one answer and 12 ms for eight. Static batching starts a batch together and returns it together, so the batch runs as many steps as its longest answer, finished answers hold their slots, and new requests wait for the whole batch. One 2,000-token report in a batch of 8 short answers held them for 24 s with 14% of the slots doing work. Continuous batching, which Orca called iteration-level scheduling, decides after every step: return finished answers, fill their slots from the queue, run the next step. Short answers come back in their own time and the slots carry only live work; Orca reported 36.9 times the throughput of FasterTransformer at the same latency on GPT-3 175B, and vLLM does this by default. For short chats and long reports on one GPU I'd use continuous batching, set the slot limit from the busiest minute and the memory each answer keeps, make sure long jobs can never take every slot, for example by capping how many run at once or running them off-peak, and watch the queue wait for short requests, not just throughput.

This season's word for the link that carries the weights from the card's memory to its adders (a10e01). Its speed sets the shortest possible step.
One pass of writing: the card reads every weight once and each answer in the step gets one more token. A 40-token answer takes 40 steps.
The tannery's own timing of its A100: a step takes 10 ms plus 0.25 ms per answer in it. 1 answer: 10.25 ms; 4: 11; 8: 12; 16: 14.
Here, the card and the program that feeds it questions and returns answers. Since 5 October it also writes the report.
Here, Rasmussen's home-made serving program: it collects questions, runs them on the card in batches and returns the answers.
One answer's room in a step. The old program always runs 8, filled or not; engineers call them slots.
Several answers written together, sharing each step's read of the weights, like a group served at one counter.
Running a batch that starts together and returns together when its longest answer ends. Newcomers wait for the next batch.
Re-packing the batch after every step: finished answers leave, waiting ones join the free slots. vLLM does it by default.
The Orca paper's name for deciding the batch after every step (iteration) instead of once per request. Continuous batching is the same idea.
Orca's way of batching only the parts of a step that answers of different lengths can share, so they can still write side by side.
The gap between one token and the next for an answer: one step (a10e02). 12 ms in a batch of 8 on the tannery's A100.
Tokens a second across all the card's work (a10e02). Slots holding finished answers add nothing to it.
A line where requests wait their turn and go out when there is room (a6e07). Here, questions waiting for a batch or a free slot.
Answer-steps that wrote a token, divided by slot-steps the card ran. Batch 1: (7 × 40 + 2,000) ÷ (8 × 2,000) = 14%.
A free, widely used serving engine for language models, with continuous batching and paged working memory (a10e03).
Software that loads a model on a card, takes requests, schedules them into steps and returns answers.
A serving system described by Yu and colleagues at OSDI '22, which introduced iteration-level scheduling and selective batching.
NVIDIA's earlier library for running transformer models fast; Orca's paper compares against it.
A language model with 175 billion weights, the one Orca's paper measured on.
The international standard for information security management. Its Annex A control 8.6 covers capacity management.
Making sure systems have the resources the work needs, now and later, by monitoring, testing and planning.

atWork: Look for a shared model server that runs fixed batches, a home-made loop or an older setup, and a long job someone moved onto it to save a card: a nightly summary, a report, a bulk rewrite. It is a common pattern: the long job lands in a batch with short chat answers, and every short answer waits for it. Ask four things. Does your server return a batch's answers together, or each as it finishes? How long is your longest answer in tokens, and how many steps does that hold a batch for? Can long jobs ever fill every slot at once? And do you watch how long short requests wait in the queue, or only throughput? A later build project will ask you to measure this. Standards-readiness note, stated conditionally and not legal advice: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, an auditor checking Annex A 8.6 (capacity management, as summarised by a third-party guide) would look for a capacity check before a new job joins a shared server, for example a replay of the busiest minute with the job added, and for monitoring that would show short requests waiting. This is not legal advice.

recall.prompt: A helpdesk serves short chat replies and a nightly 3,000-token summary on one GPU. Its home-made server takes up to 8 requests, runs them together and sends all the replies when the last one is done. At 01:00, when the summary starts, chat users wait about half a minute for one-line replies. What is happening, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The batch is returned only when its longest answer ends, so short replies finished early are held for the summary's 3,000 steps, and new requests wait for the batch to end
Schedule after every step: return finished answers at once and let waiting requests join the free slots (continuous batching, iteration-level scheduling)
A smaller batch or a faster card only shrinks the wait; a separate card removes it at a price

recall.model: The server returns a batch's replies together when its longest is done. When the summary starts it shares a batch with short replies, so they are written in under a second and then held back for the summary's 3,000 steps, and anything asked meanwhile waits for the whole batch to end. Schedule after every step instead: return each reply when it is finished and let waiting requests join the free slots, which is continuous batching, the Orca paper's iteration-level scheduling, and what vLLM does by default. A smaller batch or a faster card only shrinks the wait, because the batch still runs as long as the summary; moving the summary to a separate card removes it, at the price of a card that sits idle most of the day.

recall.prompt: On the tannery's A100 a step takes 10 ms plus 0.25 ms per answer in it, and the old program always runs 8 slots. How long does a 40-token answer take in a batch whose longest answer is 40 tokens?
recall.why: 8 slots make every step 10 + 8 × 0.25 = 12 ms, and 40 steps × 12 ms = 0.48 s. 0.41 s is the same answer alone, at 10.25 ms a step; 24 s is a batch held by a 2,000-token report.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: what is continuous batching, and why does it beat static batching for LLMs?

keyIdeas.idea: A model writes one token per step for every answer in the step, sharing one read of the weights, so batching is cheap per answer
Static batching starts and ends a batch together, so it runs at its longest answer's pace: finished answers hold their slots and newcomers wait for the whole batch

Continuous batching re-forms the batch after every step: finished answers leave and waiting ones join, so short answers don't wait for long ones and more slots do real work (Orca: iteration-level scheduling, 36.9 times the throughput)

recall.model: A model writes one token per step for every answer in the step, and the step is mostly one read of the weights, so many answers share it cheaply. Static batching starts a batch together and returns it together, so the batch runs at its longest answer's pace: finished answers hold their slots doing nothing, and new requests wait for the whole batch to end. Continuous batching, which the Orca paper calls iteration-level scheduling, decides after every step: finished answers leave and waiting ones join the free slots, then the next step runs. Short answers come back in their own time, slots carry only live work, and throughput rises; Orca reported 36.9 times FasterTransformer's at the same latency on GPT-3 175B, and vLLM does it by default.

recall.prompt: A static batch of 8 slots holds one 2,000-token report and seven 40-token answers. What share of its slot-steps writes a token?
recall.why: The batch runs 2,000 steps in 8 slots, 16,000 slot-steps. Only 7 × 40 + 2,000 = 2,280 of them write a token: 14%. 88% is 7 of 8 slots, the share holding short answers; 100% is what scheduling after every step reaches.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 2 months later. Since Wednesday 7 October the server has run vLLM, re-packing after every step, still 8 slots, and 02:00 has been quiet: screens back in about half a second. On Monday 2 November Hippolyta asked for a report for each operator's drums instead of one: eight reports of about 2,000 tokens, all at 02:00. On Tuesday 1 December at 02:00:24 Thorvaldur's screen at drum 6 finally answered. The log said 23.9 s, the same as the night in October, and drum 11 waited 19.5 s again. Rasmussen says the new engine has gone back to the old ways.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did drum 6 wait 23.9 s again, when the engine lets answers leave and join after every step? What would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The eight reports took all 8 slots at 02:00 and held them for 2,000 steps, 24 s, so the screens' questions had no free slot to join until the reports finished
Joining after every step only helps when a slot is free; the engine is working as designed, the slot limit is too small for the new load
Raise the slots (16: drum 6 back to about half a second, the reports about 24 s), or keep some slots for short questions, or spread the reports so they never fill every slot

coldCase.model: The engine is working as designed; it ran out of room. At 02:00 the eight reports reached the server first and took all 8 slots, and each needed 2,000 steps of 12 ms, 24 s. Leaving and joining after every step only helps when a slot is free, and none was until the reports finished at 24.0 s; then the screens and drum 6 joined and were answered 0.48 s later, so drum 6 waited 23.9 s, and drum 11 joined after them, 19.5 s. The slot limit is too small for the new load. Raise it: with 16 slots the screens and reports start together, drum 6 comes back after about half a second (0.50 s) and the reports take about 24 s, at a little more working memory on the card. Or keep some slots for short questions, or spread the reports across the night so they never fill every slot.
